questions.question: Name and explain the five aspects of development, showing with a South African example why appropriate-scale development matters.
questions.expected_answer: Economic development is the engine room — rising production, employment, income and investment — necessary to fund everything else but insufficient on its own. Social development is the conversion step, turning money into schools, clinics, housing, safe water and the full inclusion of women. Sustainable development follows the Brundtland definition: meeting the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs — an economy that fells its forests and drains its aquifers is spending its children's inheritance. Appropriate-scale development sizes the solution to the community: a coastal metro can justify a desalination plant and grid power, but a remote Wild Coast village is better served by rooftop solar, rainwater tanks and a hand-repairable pump, because technology must match local skills and budgets — a high-tech works nobody can repair is a monument, not development. Spatial development asks where: growth never spreads evenly, so planning must confront the gap between booming cores and neglected peripheries. An essay touching all five aspects reads as a complete answer.

questions.question: Explain the core-periphery model — core, periphery, cumulative causation, backwash and spread effects — and apply it at global, national and local scales.
questions.expected_answer: The model holds that development organises space into a powerful centre and a dependent edge. The core concentrates economic activity, investment, skills and political power; the periphery supplies raw materials and labour and receives little back; many versions add a semi-periphery in transition. The engine is cumulative causation — success recruits success, as each new plant attracts suppliers, workers and taxes that fund the infrastructure that lands the next plant. The periphery suffers backwash: its young, skilled people and savings drain coreward, leaving it older and poorer, while spread effects — investment, remittances, demand — sometimes trickle outward, and policy aims to strengthen spread while throttling backwash. Globally, the industrialised North forms the core with much of Africa, Asia and Latin America as periphery supplying minerals and crops. Nationally, Gauteng generates roughly a third of South Africa's GDP on the smallest provincial area, while former homeland districts of Limpopo and the Eastern Cape export their workers to the cities. Locally, a metro's office towers and industrial parks form the core, ringed by townships and informal settlements joined to it by long, costly commutes. Running all three scales is what turns a definition into a full answer.

questions.question: Outline Rostow's five stages, evaluate the model's main weaknesses, and use South Africa to show why the core-periphery model must accompany it.
questions.expected_answer: Rostow's stages run: traditional society (subsistence farming, little surplus); preconditions for take-off (commercial agriculture, railways, harbours, banks, an entrepreneurial class); take-off (manufacturing surges and investment passes roughly ten per cent of national income, making growth self-sustaining); drive to maturity (industry diversifies, technology spreads, cities swell); and the age of high mass consumption (households afford durables, services dominate employment). Weaknesses: the model assumes a single Western path; it ignores colonialism, since early climbers fuelled take-off partly from colonies whose development was suppressed; it ignores the core-periphery trap, in which raw-material exporters never accumulate the investment take-off demands; and it crowns mass consumption with no stage for sustainability. South Africa shows why both models are needed: its preconditions came with the mineral revolution after 1870 and take-off behind tariffs between the 1930s and 1960s, yet today insured suburbs live in mass consumption while the periphery does not — one country on several steps at once, because apartheid barred most of the population from the staircase. Core-periphery explains that spatial pattern: the homelands were legislated labour reservoirs feeding backwash to the mining core, and post-1994 zones at Saldanha Bay and Richards Bay try to bolt new cores onto the periphery. Rostow describes the timeline; core-periphery describes the map; a full evaluation uses each and criticises both.
